utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before I give you an opportunity, Mr. Kearney, to continue the examination-in-chief of Mr. Krasniqi, I'd like to say a few words. Much has been said yesterday about the annexes to the statement of this witness and to the annexes to his testimony in the Limaj case. First of all, that's a very practical matter. Annex 5 to the transcript is the same as annex 12 to the statement, and that's, as far as the Chamber could see, the only double we find in this material. Concerns have been expressed yesterday and issues have been raised in how this material was handled and should be handled, both how it was handled in the Limaj case and as it is handled now in this case. The parties have made each other aware, and of course also have made the Chamber aware, of all these concerns and issues raised. The Chamber decided yesterday not to intervene any further. The Chamber has also reviewed the annexes and found that much of what is described in these annexes, many of them are outside the temporal scope of the indictment. The Chamber did not find any direct links between some of the incidents described -- the incidents described in these documents and the incidents that are specifically mentioned in the indictment and with which the accused are charged. So upon reviewing this material, the Chamber sees no reason to change the attitude I expressed yesterday at the very end of the hearing. The Chamber leaves it to the parties how to further present this evidence - Mr. Kearney, you first - and also leaves it to the parties to assess what is needed to challenge the evidence as presented until now in this respect. Finally, I would like to mention that, of course, the debate or the discussions yesterday had a rather disruptive effect on the flow of the evidence, and the Chamber would like not to see a similar disruption of the flow of evidence when Mr. Kearney finishes the examination-in-chief of this witness. Then is -- Madam Usher, I'd like to ask you to escort the witness into the courtroom. I, meanwhile, take the opportunity to clarify the issue of the admission of the testimony of this witness in the Limaj case. As a matter of fact, I have to check that very carefully, that the number of pages mentioned by the Prosecution as the transcript of the testimony of Mr. Krasniqi in the Limaj case, I think, amounts to 255 pages, whereas the Chamber was able to find 209 pages, I think I mentioned that number yesterday, which actually is the testimony of Mr. Krasniqi. And to make it even more clear, it's transcript pages 3285 up to and including 3493. That's one. Then, since the witness has not arrived yet, there were some requests for sitting on the -- swapping on the 1st of June from afternoon to morning. Mr. Guy-Smith, I think that was a special wish. The Chamber has seriously considered it, but due to commitments of a majority of the Judges of this Chamber it, unfortunately, is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand and thank everybody for the attention to my request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then, as far as the 5th of June is concerned, there also was a matter, the parties are invited to see whether a solution could be found in calling a witness on the 5th of June which might not be of vital importance for the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have made that suggestion beforehand and we have yet to resolve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you were on your feet, at the same time the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The matter can wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony still binds you when answering questions. Mr. Kearney, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I plan also to be very brief today. I do have one matter that relates to this witness. The Chambers asked the Prosecution yesterday to prepare a formal list comparing Limaj exhibits to the 92 ter exhibits. I have those now. I passed those out to the Defence. Would the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. Then at least we have the P exhibit numbers in Limaj so we have an overview of everything, which makes it easier for Madam Registrar to get the numbers into the computer. If you hand it out, Madam Usher, Mr. Kearney I think would like to be -- yes, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There is one last matter, Your Honour, I do apologise. I didn't get a chance to speak to Mr. Kearney about this before. I was wondering what the status is with regard to those disclosure items that were discussed late yesterday, the delivery of the books --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: We called Pristina today, Your Honour. Apparently Mr. Krasniqi's correct that he gave the books to an OTP representative. He gave -- the witness did give the books to an OTP representative on Monday in Pristina. I understand that they, after that, were DHL'd or in the process of being DHL'd. The Prosecution here in The Hague has not received them yet unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that as soon as they've arrived that you immediately review that and disclose it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Of course, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'd like to follow-up very briefly on a few things that you said yesterday, the first one being at line 49 -- page 4958 of your testimony at line 6. You told us, sir, yesterday that - and I'm quoting - "but in 1998, I had almost daily contacts with the soldiers and with the operational units of the KLA." Now, I want to ask you, sir, to explain that for us, if you would. Does that mean that on a daily basis you physically called different zones or different units within Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the areas where the KLA was operating. I was in contact with the soldiers in the area where I was living; however, the contacts with our other areas or other zones were from time to time, depending on necessity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And where were you living, please, and what zone -- well, just tell us first where were you living in 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998, I lived in my native village until June; after June 1998, I lived in the villages in the Berisha mountains in Divjake, Klecke, and Novo Selle or Fshati i Ri.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: The contact you had with soldiers in other zones outside of the one you were living in, could you please tell us was that on a regular basis, a weekly basis, a monthly basis, was it dependent on facts on the ground? Please tell us more about that.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our contacts could not be weekly contacts because of the situation and because of the fightings that were going on in the summer of 1998. Whenever there was need, we had physical contacts with the zones, but these were much more infrequent. Most frequent contacts were the telephone contacts and satellite telephone contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And how often were those telephone contacts with the zones beyond the one you were living in?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say how frequent they were. They could have been weekly contacts or sometimes we could communicate twice a day, sometimes every ten days. It depended on the developments on the ground at that time. So sometimes the contacts were more frequent and sometimes they were not that frequent. This depended on the needs of the General Staff of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, these calls that you just described to the other zones, who would initiate those calls? Would it be you calling the zones, or would it be the people in the zones calling you?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended. If I needed to know about the developments on the ground, I called them, while in the case when the zones had a certain need or needed to contact us, they contacted us. The commander of the zone could contact us or people who were designated to deal with information issues, they contacted us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you say that if you needed to know about the developments on the ground, you would yourself call the zones, when you say "developments on the ground," what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the fightings that were occurring in various war zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: If there was fighting going on in a particular zone, why would you make a call to that zone? What was your purpose, Mr. Krasniqi, in making those calls?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose was to get acquainted with the situation, how the fighting occurred, and whether we had any losses on our part, and what the losses of the enemy were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: In relation to the actual fighting that was going on on the ground, when would you make these calls? Would it be the same day? The day after? Within two days? Could you give us any more detail about that, please?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever it was possible, we called them the same day. When it was not possible, we communicated the next day. But as I said, this communication was via satellite telephone. We did not have any other possibilities to communicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, when you say that when it was possible we called them the same day," who do you refer to when you say "we," please?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We who were working in the General Staff, and the General Staff has -- had a limited administration body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier that on occasion the commander - this is at line 17, page 6 - "the commander of the zone would contact us or people who were designated to deal with information issues, they contacted us." What would those people, either the commanders in the zones or their designees call you about?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would call us to inform us about the situation, and they would ask for assistance and things like these.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you say they would ask you for assistance, what do you mean by that, Mr. Krasniqi? What kind of assistance would zone commanders ask you for?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The zone commanders, but even other units, smaller combat units, whenever they would be attacked by enemy forces the -- and the forces of that unit were limited, they asked for assistance, for reinforcement by other units that were closer to the area of the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier the general time-period for these communications being, I think, the summer of 1998. Can you be more specific, please, about what time-period you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the time-period after June 1998, end of July, August, and September where the major fighting occurred. Everybody knows about the offensive of 1998, the summer offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: How about the period before July of 1998, the first half, if you will, of 1998? Describe, please, for us the communication you had with the zones during that period.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I speak about this, we have to make a distinction between the various development stages of the army. Before summer 1998, the KLA was a guerilla army. It had limited access to areas and limited number of soldiers. It was an army that was a guerilla army with guerilla units that used the hit-and-run tactics. These units had a number of people, but this number was limited, and they all acted clandestinely. After February 1998, 28th of February, 1998, when 24 people were massacred in Likoshan and Qirez, and after the events of the 5th, 6th, and 7th of March, 1998, people wanted to join the KLA en masse and this was the time when the General Staff did not have enough senior officers to respond to this request. Many people joined the KLA and various units of the villages joined the KLA, but they were outside the control and the structures, the normal structures of the KLA. This -- the army was mostly of a voluntary and people's army character, and people who had been appointed as responsible persons for certain areas were also asked to contact the KLA. So, for example, the General Staff at various times had to have these talks with representatives of villages who sometimes had only hunting guns at their disposal, and we wanted them to become part of a more organised structure led by the General Staff. So we can say that in -- during the period June, July, and August we had this people's army, a voluntary army, and the first attempts to have a better-organised army were being made at that time. But then the summer offensive started, so it was impossible to have this better organisation of the KLA. The summer offensive thwarted our efforts to better organise ourselves. So until October 1998, we were not able to consolidate the KLA, while in November 1998 we had a quieter period. The Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement was signed, and we exploited this quieter period to organise ourselves. We had the companies, the battalions, and the brigades of the KLA. So the organisation and the discipline were better towards the latter part of the year than the beginning of the year. But still, it was far from being a well-organised army in the proper military sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, thank you for that answer, but I'd like, if I may, to draw your attention back to the time-period after the attacks you mentioned in February and early March of 1998. I want to ask you simply if, after those attacks, your communication with the subzones increased, the General Staff's communication with the subzones increased?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the increase in the numbers of the KLA, the communications increased as well. But there were armed groups of villagers who were outside of this control, so we had to work in various directions at the same time. But we did not have the manpower to work with all of them. So I wouldn't say that we had the proper communication. We communicated in the -- all the areas as we should have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: With regard to the Dukagjin Zone in particular, beginning in March of 1998, who did you have contact with within that zone? Who did you talk to, please?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I did not communicate with anyone in the Dukagjini Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did anyone in the General Staff contact with -- have contact with people in the Dukagjini Zone at that time, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time I cannot say who communicated with them. I can only say -- I can only speak of the period after June 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And after June of 1998, who did you contact -- who did you have contact with within the Dukagjini Zone when you were calling them on behalf of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We also contacted in other ways, not only by telephone. So in June 1998, for example, I contacted with Lahi Brahimaj; he was also a member of the General Staff of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I'm referring now to KLA soldiers on the ground in Dukagjini Zone, beginning in June of 1998. Who did you have contact with, please?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I contacted Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Was he the only person within the Dukagjini Zone that you ever talked to after June of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the person that I knew and the person I communicated with, and I think he was responsible for the area at that time. Later on I also contacted Mr. Ramush Haradinaj, the commander of the zone. I think it was only once, end of June or beginning of July, but I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Earlier you told us that after June of 1998 you had -- you began to have more regular contact with the zones, and you described for us the communications you had with people on the ground about operational detail. I'd like to ask you, after June of 1998, when you received information from operational units on the ground, what did you do with that information, sir, as a member of the General Staff? Did you publish it? Did you record it somehow? What did you do with that information?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information did not come only to us. The information about the developments on the ground went also to the media, international media and Albanian media. Of course we had other duties. We had organisational duties as well, and we also compiled political statements where we set out all the strategy and the political opinions of the KLA, but also we reflected in those statements the fighting that was occurring at the time in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you reflected the fighting that was ongoing in Kosovo in those statements, did you base those statements in part on information you received from the zones from the soldiers on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our political stand had been formed already, even before these actions and combat operations occurred. We had compiled these political statements to boost the morale of the members of the KLA, of the citizens of Kosova. We wanted to gain the respect of the citizens of Kosova and also inform the international community about the right and just war that the Kosovo Liberation Army was waging.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'm not just talking about your political or your policy statements; I'm referring to press releases, communiques, that were made after June of 1998. Did you incorporate data that you had learned from the soldiers you talked to on the ground into those releases and communiques?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communiques included information from the fighting on the terrain, sometimes maybe somewhat exaggerated, but this was because of the propaganda campaign that we were waging and we wanted to inform the public opinion. As I said, sometimes we exaggerated our successes and exaggerated enemy's losses, while trying to diminish our losses and our casualties; that was the purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. And I'm aware of your propaganda role as well as you talked about -- as you defined it yesterday. But I want to ask you: When you were reporting operational details in your statements to the press, in your communiques, I understand that the -- the scope and magnitude of some of these details were exaggerated. But the basic facts about date, location, time, were those accurate, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say whether everything was accurate. We were trying to describe the actions that were taking place on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, my question is even more simple than that. I just want to ask you: Were there times in your communiques where you just completely invented a battle that never happened or completely invented or just created an incident that was completely untrue that had no basis in fact?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not release any announcements about facts that did not exist or occur. I tried to reflect on the events that really happened, but trying to have this optimistic tone and trying probably to exaggerate a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Just a brief question, Mr. Krasniqi. Before you were appointed spokesman for the KLA on 11 June 1998, who was the spokesperson before you took that job? Did you have a predecessor?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't anybody who was a predecessor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Were there -- before you took sole responsibility of the job, were there several people who -- on the General Staff who dealt with the media or issued releases?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that period, it was the Zeri i Kosoves newspaper who acted as the political wing of the KLA and they published releases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And were those then adopted by the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already explained yesterday that the General Staff during this period had some members in Kosova, but many other members were in Switzerland and Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that information, Mr. Krasniqi, but I want to ask you again: You told us yesterday that all the annexes to your statement were communications or reports that accurately reflected statements that were issued by the UCK General Staff. I'd like to ask you: How did this -- how did the General Staff interact with Zeri i Kosoves?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the time that I was appointed spokesperson, we communicated with Zeri i Kosoves by satellite telephone. I don't know how they communicated before my time. Maybe they used another means of communication, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: But my question is more basic: Who was the person who actually had contact with Zeri i Kosoves? Who called them on the phone?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before my time as a spokesperson, I don't know; but when I became a spokesperson, it was me mainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: But someone from the General Staff called them with information about operations on the ground; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat myself. As for the earlier period, I don't know; but as of the time when I became the spokesperson, I did this job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I'm not asking you for a name, Mr. Krasniqi, but I'm just asking you: Did members of the KLA General Staff contact Zeri i Kosoves before you became spokesperson in June of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most probably yes, because as I said Zeri i Kosoves in a way was a body of the Kosova People's Movement, but before June 1998, before the consolidation of the General Staff, the LPK and Zeri i Kosoves acted as the political wing of the Kosova Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to ask you a little bit about the time-period after you became spokesperson. The annexes that you have in front of you, do you still have the book of annexes in front of you, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If not, they should be given to Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you. These are now part of Exhibit 328, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: The last six of these annexes, 14 through 19, were they statements or interviews made by you after you became the KLA press person? Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: One of those annexes attached to Exhibit 328 - this is annex 12, strike that, this is annex 18 - is part of a long interview you gave to Koha Ditore in July of 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: As a spokesperson for the Kosovo Liberation Army, what was your purpose in giving that interview, please?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to that time, the KLA had not revealed to that extent its political programme and had not communicated directly with the public information media and as a spokesperson, as -- lacking a spokesperson or a figure that would represent the KLA in this time. So this was a purpose to familiarise the public opinion about the political programme and the purpose of the KLA's war. Until that time, the information about the KLA was limited and even the citizens of Kosova had acquainted that information through media. So now there existed an address, both for the public opinion and for a media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, was there a reason that you chose Koha Ditore as the outlet to issue this communication regarding the political programme of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Koha Ditore was the most-read newspaper at that time in Kosova. And at the same time, it was the newspaper that in one way or another supported the most the activities of the KLA, in addition to Zeri i Kosoves that was published in Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did this newspaper have readership in Kosovo outside of Pristina itself?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, there were readers both in Kosova and in the diaspora, in Switzerland and in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Was this newspaper read by KLA soldiers themselves who were engaged in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The newspapers could not penetrate that easily in combat zones, but they did; and when they did, of course they were read.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Who did you wish to communicate your -- the KLA's political programme to? Was it -- was it Albanians living in Kosovo? Was it Serbs in Kosovo? Was it the international community? Who did you intend to receive this -- this message you were giving to Koha Ditore in July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main audience was the Albanian people inside Kosova and abroad. Of course Koha Ditore at that time was a prestigious newspaper, well-known, and was read regularly by international representatives in Kosova. As for the international opinion is concerned, after this interview I had interviews also with a journalist from CNN, BBC, and other media. However, we informed the public opinion of the political programme of the KLA through political statements and through -- that were published in Deutsche Welle and BBC and interviews with these agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'm almost done here. This -- under annex 18, this exhibit, you have told us already that this is a full and accurate reflection of the interview you gave to Koha Ditore. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'd like to direct your attention to the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: For the Court, again, this is Exhibit 328, pages 82 through 88 of the original 65 ter number which is 1346, if that helps. I wonder if we could go to the last page of this document in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, this page has on it a series of questions by Koha Ditore and answers by yourself. I want to direct your attention, if I may, to the approximate middle of the page, and there's a clause in the lower portion of the large or the long answer you give on that page which begins: "Even if some people have suffered ..." Can you find that, please, for us and let us know when you're there.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very small font. Can you tell me which line it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. Krasniqi, I can read it out for you if that will help you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, I have not found it yet, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, there are page numbers on P328, 94 pages in total. Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: This is the ERN number on the document, Your Honour, if the Court can see that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: -- The original ERN was 0 -- U0038589 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it. Could you then please guide us where approximately to find the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: There is a highlighted passage there on the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'm going to read you a few lines -- a few sentences from this statement. I'm going to ask you first if -- and then ask you if you can find those. "We do not go in for kidnapping. Even if some people have suffered, these have been more Albanian collaborators than Serbian civilians. We do not deal with civilians, and we return those whom we take as prisoners of war. A few days ago we handed over two Serbs originating from Croatia to the International Red Cross" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, can you find that passage?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The font is very small. I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Do you see the words "International Red Cross" on that page? Mr. Krasniqi, if it helps you, this is approximately two paragraphs up from the very bottom of the interview, the very end of the interview. In that location, there's a sentence where the words "International Red Cross" are mentioned." Mr. Krasniqi, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: This document is being brought up on e-court. Is that correct? Perhaps at this time, Your Honour, with the Court's permission I can just read out this paragraph or we can do it on re-direct and I will endeavour to get a clearer copy for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'm just going to read it out to you and ask you if you recognise your own words in this interview. Mr. Krasniqi, do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: "Even if some people have suffered, these have been more Albanian collaborators than Serbian civilians" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, when you read, please slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're developing a speed which is -- cannot be followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise that sentence I just read to you, Mr. Krasniqi, as being your own words?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember saying it exactly as it is. I have to see it first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps this is an issue that we can better take up in re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It must not be that difficult to find that portion, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that in the Albanian original the relevant passage is in the last column on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just seek the assistance of the interpreters. Is that approximately at where the upper arm on the picture is?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Krasniqi, you'll find that portion you see at your right-hand side, you see a picture of a person. Look in the last column, approximately at the level where the upper arm of that person is and tell us whether you could find the -- and does the witness have it in black and white because it's -- doesn't make it any clearer, I would say. You found it, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's good. Then could you please read the portion that was just read to you by Mr. Kearney. Since the witness has found it, Mr. Kearney, you can put your question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, again I'm going to read out to you four consecutive sentences from that text. I'll do it very slowly. At the end of it I'm going to ask you if you recognise those words. "We do not go in for kidnapping. Even if some people have suffered, these have been more Albanian collaborators than Serbian civilians. We do not deal with civilians and we return those whom we take as prisoners of war. A few days ago we handed over two Serbs originating from Croatia to the International Red Cross. Those we have kidnapped are either announced in a list or reported to be executed, but we do not behave in a base fashion like Serbia." My question is: Do you see those words, Mr. Krasniqi, in that document?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give an opportunity to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I thought Your Honour had a matter you wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I just wanted to consult with my colleagues for a second. Mr. Krasniqi, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Emmerson, who is counsel for Mr. Haradinaj. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I deal with two administrative matters. I noticed that yesterday afternoon when certain questions were asked which involved reference to the Limaj transcript, that Your Honours were obliged to follow it from the screen. And since I'm going to be touching on one or two passages, I've had hard copies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least I took the Limaj transcript with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I have had some hard copies prepared for the Bench, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if you provide them to us, then it will certainly assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It makes for a smoother cross-examination. And the other document that I wanted, if I may, to provide to you and to the witness is a record of an interview conducted with this witness by OTP investigators on the 4th of May, 2004. Now, there is an Albanian translation which I'm having handed to the witness, and then the English original which is being handed to Your Honours and a copy is available for Mr. Kearney, although I imagine he has it already. And for the record, those investigator notes are Defence document 1D410081, although I don't at this stage ask either that they be marked for identification or tendered. But if they're to be brought up on the screen, that is their identification number. I think hard copies have been provided to the translation booths. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I want to start, if I may, by asking you some questions about the General Staff itself. And I think you have given evidence in the past and confirmed it to us, I believe, that you joined the General Staff yourself sometime at the end of 1996 or the beginning of 1997. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want, if I may, please, to have a sense of what that meant in reality so that the Trial Chamber has a picture of what state of organisation the body describing itself as a General Staff was in when you joined it. First of all, you came to join the General Staff how exactly, yourself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Just very briefly, and I don't want to interrupt the cross-examination. My colleague mentioned a statement to us earlier, was that a statement made by this witness to the Defence and --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: It was not?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No I meant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He's referring to the investigator's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I meant a statement made to us in court, in this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So just to repeat my question, Mr. Krasniqi, how did you, yourself, come to join this group of people styling themselves a General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This requires a broader explanation, how I came to join. I was a political prisoner in -- from 1981 until 1991. In 1991, late 1991, there was an armed attack against the Jashari family and there were fighting between the members of the Adem Jashari family and the Serbian police. In July 1991, I was released from prison and in the autumn of that year I engaged in politics. I became at that time a member of the Democratic League of Kosova. During that fighting on the 30th of December, 1991, that very night, I contacted, in Polac, Adem Jashari and his armed formation. I'm saying this because my contacts with the men from the operations, such as Adem Jashari at the time who had started the preparations for armed uprising as early as in the 1990s, I was familiar with these people. I had contacts with them. I contacted and knew other persons of this type, former political prisoners. In 1993, several members of the LPK were arrested. During this time, there were people who were ready to form and establish the political wing of the LPK. During this time-period, I was in contact with both political and operational staff, but these contacts were very rare, not that frequent, because I was a political activist acting illegally --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Legally, correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- And I was being persecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, forgive me for interrupting your answer. The question that I want to ask you to focus on is specifically asking about the end of 1996 and the beginning of 1997 when you came to join this group of people calling themselves a General Staff. Now, specifically in relation to that process, who asked you to be a member of the General Staff or did you ask yourself?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I had contacts with KLA people even earlier, but because of the fact that the KLA was getting better organised, especially the operational part, I was the political person who was familiar with the developments in Kosova. And they decided, due to this better organisation and with a purpose of establishing the political wing, the commander of the KLA, Adem Jashari, requested me that I became member of the KLA General Staff and deal mainly with the political staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So Adem Jashari asked you to join and to take responsibility for political rather than operational and military matters; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And at that time in 1997, is it right that you didn't know who the other members of the General Staff were?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you give us a sense of how many people there were who claimed to be members of the General Staff in total, that is, including those you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during this period of time, the General Staff consisted of approximately ten persons but not all of them knew each other because some were acting illegally, some legally, some were abroad. Basically we had to suit the conditions we were operating in.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand, but just so that we have a picture. If you didn't know who a number of these people were, presumably you had no means of communicating with them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we ask the witness to answer that question, I noticed that you started your question about the end of 1996/early 1997, and in the next question you said: "At that time in 1997" --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which seems to cover at least a larger time-period, exclude 1996. I don't know whether that has been sufficiently --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- clear and whether your last question would be limited to the initial period you mentioned or whether it would cover the whole of 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'll clarify that. I take Your Honour's point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did it remain the position for the whole of 1997 that there were people amongst that ten whose names and identities you did not know at that time? Did that remain the position throughout 1997?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that you did not know the names of more than half or less than half of the other members of the body calling itself the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say now because I know all of them now, but at the time I did not know some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And I think you knew, obviously, Adem Jashari, is that correct, and you knew he was a member --

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you knew Sokol Bashota and Rexhep Selimi. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Sokol at the time but not Rexhep.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So you knew Adem Jashari and Sokol Bashota. Did you know Hashim Thaqi at the time by name?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So did you know all three of them were members of the General Staff in 1997, is that something you knew at that time?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, know the names of any other members of the General Staff at that time, Mr. Krasniqi, during 1997?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of Azem Syla being a member in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. And is that a total of the names you then knew at that time?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So if there were ten altogether, you knew the names of five including yourself. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And were those five all inside Kosovo or were they themselves spread across Kosovo and Albania?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except Azem and Hashim Thaqi, the rest were in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Azem and Hashim would go to Albania and Switzerland. They remained in Kosovo for a limited period of time. Or they -- when they came, they acted clandestinely.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mention -- I say illegal but I mean clandestine.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So essentially do we have -- so essentially, Mr. Krasniqi, can you confirm then that the position is this: There were three people, including yourself, who were based inside Kosovo during 1997 who you knew to be members of the General Staff. There were two who were based outside Kosovo who you knew to be members of the General Staff. And there were five other members of the General Staff whose identity you did not know. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And those five were distributed across what is described as the diaspora, Switzerland, Germany, the United States, France, Scandinavian countries; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They lived in the western states. These were citizens of Kosova that had left Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And do you know how any of them came to be selected for the so-called General Staff during that period?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not during 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And presumably, if you didn't know who these people were, you can't have had much in the way of direct communication with them, could you, during 1997?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, these were people I didn't know so I did not communicate with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So was it really the three of you, Mr. Krasniqi, that had contact with each other during 1997, Mr. Jashari, Mr. Bashota, and yourself? Is that really what it came down to as far as you could, yourself, communicate with other people?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that during this period I could not communicate regularly with these people that went to Albania and Switzerland, I mean Azem Syla and Hashim Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Now, correct me if I am wrong, but during 1997 you didn't really have formal meetings of the General Staff, did you?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the people that were inside Kosova, we used to contact with them. But even the people who were outside Kosova contacted with the ones inside Kosova. So those of us who were in Kosova communicated with each other. We tried to communicate. And some other people in Kosova who knew the people that were outside might have communicated with them. Those were the possibilities of communication that we had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: They might have, Mr. Krasniqi, but do you know whether, for example, there was any form of formal communication with the five individuals whose identities you did not then know?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any contact with people I didn't know, because I was one of the youngest or the newest members of the General Staff in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let's move, if we may, to the first half of 1998. Let's take it to the middle of 1998. How many members of the General Staff were by then inside Kosovo on a permanent basis?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the number varied, about seven or eight. Then later the General Staff expanded with a -- including the zone commanders. So the number of the members of the General Staff increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That was sometime later, was it. When did that occur?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This happened after November 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not concerned with that period. Going back to June of 1998, were there still people then who were members of the General Staff outside Kosovo whose identities you did not know?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And within Kosovo, is it right that the General Staff was broken up; in other words, you were not -- those of you who were members of the General Staff were not located in any one building. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Because we could not have one safe area where the General Staff could stay for a longer time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. But not only did members of the General Staff move around, but they moved around separately from one another, did they not?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, usually they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, again, that takes us up to June and we know that on the 11th of June you took over a formal spokesman role. I want to look, if I may, with you for a moment at the position with these communiques up until that time. Is it right, Mr. Krasniqi, that many of these communiques were issued from the diaspora, and in particular from Switzerland during 1997?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The communiques were released sometimes from Switzerland, sometimes from Albania as well. But I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And were they then being released by people whose identities you did not know?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communiques were issued by people I didn't know. I didn't know their identity at the time when those communiques were written.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And does that apply also --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Two more questions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- to 1998, up till June?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I'm going to state an objection. I would ask counsel to be more particular or precise in what communiques he's referring to. His earlier words were all-inclusive and I ask that we have more precision in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, it was entirely precise. "All of the communiques" is what I put and that's what the witness answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I repeat the question, please, Mr. Krasniqi, was it also the position up to the 11th of June that the communiques that were issued on behalf of the KLA General Staff were being issued from the diaspora by people who you did not know?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already said, I don't know who issued those communiques up till that time because I didn't know those people. But I have to say that the political statement that was issued in April 1998, I was one of the authors of that statement. It was written by me and other members of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to come to that distinction between the political statements and the communiques after the break. I've just got one final question. Does it follow from the answer that you've just given us, Mr. Krasniqi, that in respect of the communiques reporting military action, you had no contact whatsoever with the authors of those communiques before they were written?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. Emmerson. Mr. Kearney, you made an objection. It looked as if Mr. Emmerson was ruling on it. I didn't do it yet. It would be next time better, Mr. Emmerson, if you would like to respond, no problem. But what happened, as a matter of fact, so I will rule on your objection. The objection is denied because exactly the same happened here as what happened yesterday when you said about a question, I think it covered the whole of 1998. The Defence said: Could you please be more specific. I then explained to the Defence that depending on the answer there might need -- might be need to seek more specificity. Exactly the same thing happened here, Mr. Emmerson was actually putting a question covering all the communiques he had mentioned up till that moment. You were seeking more specificity, whereas that might have been the next question. So therefore, just as I indicated yesterday, that the Defence should give it some time to first hear the answer and not to seek specificity already when a question is phrased in very general terms. I think that the same would be -- would apply for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you. That's a point well taken, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Emmerson, even a ruling on such a matter needs sometimes a bit of explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you have done that already. We will resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, you were drawing a distinction before the break between political statements and communiques. Can I put a suggestion to you in that context, that overall there were three ways by which individuals connected with General Staff communicated with the media and the public. First of all, there were direct interviews conducted with you after the 11th of June but not before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And secondly, there were a series of political statements published in the name of the KLA General Staff, both before and after your appointment as the spokesman on the 11th of June; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but there were only few before 11th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But you mentioned, I think, one in April 1998. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you were closely involved, I think, in the drafting of those political statements; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then third -- in the third category are what has been described here as communiques which were, I think, issued not by the political wing in which you were involved, but by members of what were described as the operational wing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is mainly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you've told us, I think, that certainly up to the time of your appointment you had no contact with the people drafting those communiques before they were drafted and sent out. Can I ask you this: After your appointment on the 11th of June, was that still the position? Did those people still send out communiques -- these communiques recording military activity without your direct involvement; in other words, with no contact with you about the content of the communique after the 11th of June?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 11th of June, in the majority of cases, we were aware of the text of the communiques.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When you say "we," I'm asking, if I may, specifically about you. Were you aware --

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Myself and other members of the staff responsible for information --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for communication with the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. The 11th of June becomes the distinction date as far as you are concerned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Even after that, Mr. Krasniqi, did you personally author any of the communiques? Did you actually write the words that appeared in the communiques yourself?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These communiques, I was the author of them during the time when the offensives were at their highest peak and when there were difficulties for us as members of the General Staff to assemble. There are many occasions, I don't remember every one of them, but I, on those occasions, drafted the communiques on the basis of the information I received from the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That was the next question I was going to come to. You've given us some information that the content of the communiques came from information that was derived from the ground. And I think in your testimony in Limaj you used the expression "grass roots". First of all, specifically as regards the Dukagjini area, can I suggest to you that you, apart from the incident where you described meeting Mr. Haradinaj, which I'll come back to, you did not have telephone communication with him before the autumn of 1998 whilst you were in Kosovo. Is that a suggestion with which you would agree?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in terms of the information that was provided to you after the 11th of June and the information that was put into the communiques, I think you have said on a number of occasions, both in your testimony in this court and in your testimony in the Limaj case, that really the primary purpose of those communiques issued after the 11th of June, as well as those issued before, the primary purpose was what you have described as propaganda. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And just so that we're clear, part of the purpose -- part of the propaganda purpose was to raise morale of the civilian population; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Part was to encourage recruitment into the ranks of the KLA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And as a result, I think you've confirmed already, the methodology was to talk up military successes and talk down military failures; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I can say that there existed two KLAs, one on paper and one on the ground. That's why I'm saying it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And on a number of occasions in your testimony in Limaj, you observed to the Judges there that you were unhappy about the idea of these communiques being taken as evidence of the facts contained within them. Is that because you are concerned that they present a misleading picture?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time and even nowadays, I continue to think that in absence of facts the Court is taking into consideration propaganda material. In my opinion, this material should not be used in delivering justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, to what extent material that is produced for purposes of propaganda should be taken into consideration in whatever determination this Court or any Court would have to make is up to the Court. And I would like you to refrain from commenting on what we should and we should not use. Just to avoid whatever misunderstanding there may be, the Chamber, even if it considers material that was produced for propaganda reasons, using such material does not mean that the Chamber would adopt whatever has been put to the public as propaganda. Of course the Chamber, as you may have noticed earlier today, would carefully try to distinguish between what are facts, because even in propaganda sometimes facts are reflected, and what could not be considered to be facts. So I would invite you to refrain from giving us guidance as how and what to use in order to deliver justice because the suggestion is clearly there that if we would use any of these communiques that we would not deliver justice, and that is a comment which is not appropriate for a witness to make. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I just want to put to you a specific from the testimony that you gave in Limaj in this regard from page 3421, line 11. You said this in answer to a question from counsel. You said: "I agree that we had to speak about successes even when there wasn't any successes to speak about." Is that something which happened in the communiques that you issued?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And was that same pattern reflected in the interviews that you gave, Mr. Krasniqi, the interviews you gave to the media?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I wonder if you could have a look at the document that I handed to you or had handed to you at the beginning of my cross-examination, which is a series of notes of an interview conducted with you by the Office of the Prosecution in May 2004. Now, first of all, just to be clear as to what this document is, I'm going to put certain propositions to you, Mr. Krasniqi, perhaps you would let me run right through them and then either confirm or contradict what I put to you. I think you were summoned by the Office of the Prosecution and required to attend for an interview that took place on the 4th of May, 2004. The interview was tape recorded, but it was later discovered that due to a technical fault the tape was not capable of being listened to. And as a result, these notes were produced from contemporaneous notes taken during the investigation. They were then translated into Albanian and you were given a copy to approve, and you initialled an Albanian copy to indicate the correctness of the contents of those notes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I just want to look at some of the passages in these notes, if I may. Could you turn to paragraphs 19 and 20. If I can just introduce those paragraphs to you, Mr. Krasniqi, to orientate you in the interview without taking time on the exhibit. You were being questioned there about an interview that you gave to Der Spiegel magazine on the 6th of July, 1998, in which you had claimed that the KLA was in possession of heavy weaponry and poised to move in and take control of Pristina. Now, first of all, Mr. Krasniqi, can you confirm, please, that that was not, in fact, the position on the 6th of July, 1998; the KLA was not, in fact, in a position in which it was seriously poised to take control of Pristina, was it?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It wasn't. You agree with the suggestion that I'm putting to you?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you're recorded as having said this in relation to that interview in the notes of the interview with the Prosecution. "When questioned regarding the statements concerning heavy or advanced weaponry, Mr. Krasniqi indicated that he made the statements but that these statements were made as part of a propaganda campaign or, in his words, as a 'Special war' or 'Psychological war'." It then goes on at paragraph 20: "The KLA General Staff carried out this propaganda campaign to present the KLA as more organised than it might have been and in this way gain credibility." Pausing there for a moment. Is that an accurate reflection of the approach you took to the Der Spiegel article or interview?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And is it an accurate reflection of the approach you took to all interviews with the media, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You can put those notes to one side for the moment; I'll come back to them in a little while. Earlier this afternoon, Mr. Kearney concluded his cross-examination by asking you about a passage in a lengthy interview that was published in Koha Ditore on the 11th and 12th of July. He took you, I think, to the second half of that two-day article which was annex 18 to your witness statement. You were asked some questions in the Limaj trial about the first half of that interview published on the 11th of July, 1998, which is annex 17 to your witness statement, and commenting on that interview at transcript page 3377 you said this, and I quote: "By means of this material we sought to convey the idea even though sometimes we exaggerated the reality, but the purpose was to win over the support of the citizens of Kosovo, to win over the support of the entire Albanian public, as well as that of the international public. So as I said, this is a material which aimed at presenting the level of organisation of the KLA at a higher level which was not the case in reality." And I'm asking you, please, first of all to confirm that that was the approach you took to the whole of that interview with Koha Ditore, published across two days on the 11th and 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was my stance and the stance of the General Staff at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what I want to do now is to move on to ask you some questions which might give us some assistance at distinguishing between, first of all, fact and propaganda, and then where fact is related in some of these documents, the reliability of the information on which it is based. And the extent to which you may or may not be able to help us with that. Could I ask you, please, to look at -- just at two short examples. Annex 2 in the little blue file which is a newspaper report from Koha Ditore for the 8th of August, 1997, of a statement issued in the name of the KLA. And the passage I want you to look at in the -- have you got -- you've got the Albanian document there. If you could look in the Albanian, five lines down from the main text you will find the letters UCK in square brackets. Do you see that? Five lines down in the main text do you see the letters UCK in square brackets?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll just read the English translation. "'The Kosovo Liberation Army' [UCK] claims responsibility for recent armed incidents in Kosovo, in which two Serbian policemen and two Albanian civilians were injured." That, I think you can confirm, is a comment by the newspaper rather than a quotation from the communique, that sentence. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There is then a quotation from the communique itself. "This communique states: 'By a decision of the UCK Central Staff made on 3 and 4 August, our guerilla units carried out three armed operations against the occupiers and their collaborators.'" Just pause there, please. Can I ask you now: Do you have any personal knowledge of the two Serbian policemen who were injured or that are referred to as having been injured? Do you know who they were or where they were injured?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Before the witness answers this question --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: -- Mr. Emmerson, may I ask you, are we in August 1997?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, do you now know who those two Serbian policemen were or where they were injured?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Or the two Albanian civilians that were injured, do you know who they were or where and in what circumstances they were injured?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge about this, but as I said earlier some of the information we got was from the media itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand. And please, don't think I'm criticising you in any way. It's just to get some sense of what you can really help the Trial Chamber with in terms of content. And where the communique is quoted as referring to three armed operations that were authorised on the 3rd and 4th of August, do you know what those three armed operations were? Can you tell us now what those three armed operations were from your own knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I did not have any knowledge about these operations. I may know of them today, but not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. Could you look, please, at annex 9 which is a little later in time. This is a report in Pristina Bujku on the 11th of March, 1998, which reports a further communique and quotes it. Do you have that? Just give me one moment.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, just one moment, if I may. Can you help us with this, Mr. Krasniqi. Can you see a headline in the Albanian news item that reads or makes reference to the UCK staff issuing a communique on military engagements? Is it the bottom right-hand box, is it, in the newspaper article?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you look, please, there is a quotation there looking at the bottom of the first column. Can I read to you the English translation. It's the third paragraph in inverted commas in the English translation and I believe it is the last paragraph in the first column, but correct me if I'm wrong. I'm sorry, I do apologise, it's not. It's the first full paragraph in the second column, Mr. Krasniqi, that's where I need to direct your attention to. It reads: "'The UCK's military formations also engaged occupation forces in the Llap region in the area between Decan, Gjakove, and Kline, and between Malisheve and Rahovec crossing from the Lumihat region. There were also engagements on a line stretching from Decan to Peje [Pec].'" Is that what the text says in the Albanian version?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And again the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, the inverted commas are difficult for me to find in the original, whereas --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Some moments -- for example, in the middle of the first column it's clear that it starts there with inverted commas not knowing exactly where it stops, but I have some difficulties in identifying inverted commas in the part you just read.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm afraid the quality of the copy is -- certainly my copy is very poor. It has a lot of black markings that are rather difficult to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course I enlarged it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think, yes, it does appear as those the inverted commas begin the quotation and are not repeated on each subparagraph in the original in the way that they are in the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Let me just compare with the translation to see. Yes, well, we need to take a closer look but especially the inverted commas before "The UCK's military also engaged... " There I have difficulties in identifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That being on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, all I want to establish from you is whether you're now able to give us the specifics of some of these reported engagements, and in particular in the passage I directed your attention to, there is a reference to the UCK military formations engaging occupation forces between Decan, Gjakove, and Kline, and also engagements on a line stretching from Decan to Peje. First of all, do you now know, that's the first part of my question, do you now know exactly where or when those specific engagements occurred, the numbers of forces involved, and the nature of the engagements? Is that something you are able to tell us here today, the specifics, or not?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't because at this time, before the 11th of March, on the 8th, 9th, and the 10th of March, the funeral of the people killed in Prekaze was organised. So we were engaged in Drenica mainly, and I don't know about developments outside the Drenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. But again, with information percolating up from the ground, I mean, do you accept that there is a risk of local fighters exaggerating the successes of the KLA and downplaying its losses in communicating information to the General Staff as well as a risk of the General Staff distorting the information in the communiques being published?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were cases, for example, when an attack was launched on the enemy forces from a distance and the communique spoke about a success that, in fact, was not such. The event might have happened, the -- the event occurred, but we exaggerated it a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But would you also agree, Mr. Krasniqi, that unless we know who it was that provided the information to the General Staff in the first place, there's a risk that even the information that the General Staff received involved inaccuracies or distortions?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There could have been distortions, but in addition to the communiques also the media were given information about the same events.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that. But it was a feature, wasn't it, of the media coverage of Kosovo that different newspapers would distort the facts of particular issues, depending upon whether they were pro-Serb or pro-Albanian as well. It was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this calls for speculation on behalf of this witness and it's compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
