utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson, the objection is sustained. Would you please try to find a factual basis for some of the matters you put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I formulate a question and see if there's an objection to it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Before you answer this question, take a pause, Mr. Krasniqi. Did you come across occasions during your time in Kosovo in 1998 where the same incident would be reported in pro-Serbian newspapers in a manner completely different to the way in which that same incident was reported in pro-Albanian newspapers?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I don't think there is a person in the courtroom who doesn't have some experience in this regard, but there is no relevance unless the witness is talking about a specific media report, about a specific incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- first, there's no reason to ask for any specifics if the witness never saw such a thing. So the witness -- would you please answer the question, that is whether you came across in Kosovo in 1998 where the same incident would be reported in pro-Serbian newspaper in a manner completely different to the way in which that same incident was reported in pro-Albanian newspapers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to clarify here that there were no pro-Serb newspapers in Kosova at the time, and the Albanian newspapers were limited. But however, there were media, Serb media, that were followed in Kosovo and there were discrepancies between the Serb media and the Albanian media very often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want to ask you now, if I may, some questions about the emergence of the organisation of the KLA in the period between the Likoshan and Prekaze incident, that is to say, the early part of March, and the end of August. That's the period I want you to focus on, please, from early to mid-March at one end and the end of August to another -- at the other. You used in your testimony in Limaj on a number of occasions, you used the word "horizontal" to describe the way in which the organisation of the KLA began to emerge during that period. And it's that concept of horizontal development that I want to explore with you. After those attacks in the end of February and the beginning of March, is it right that in many parts of Kosovo, but particularly in Drenica and Dukagjin, villages began to start trying to organise themselves into village defence units. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what happened and that's what I said in the Limaj case. I also mentioned something about this today.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this is something that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And during that period, initially arms were scarce and people were using hunting rifles and any type of weaponry they could get their hands on. Is that generally the picture?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: They would organise rotas amongst themselves to keep watch; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And dig trenches and fortifications around their villages?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And they would elect their own village commanders; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the majority of the cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so that we're clear, none of this was centrally organised, was it? These villages were organising themselves spontaneously by and large, that was the pattern. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But the General Staff, and perhaps local commanders, would try to organise them in one form or another to bring them into, over time and to a greater extent over that period, to bring them into the KLA. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what we were engaged in doing during the summer of 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I would like to seek a clarification of one of the previous answers of the witness. Mr. Krasniqi, Mr. Emmerson asked you: "They would elect their own village commanders; is that right?" And then you said: "In the majority of the cases, yes." Could you tell us what happened in the minority of the cases, which you apparently excluded from your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the cases where the KLA was better organised in a certain village or a certain area, the commander was not elected by the villagers. But in many cases, during the summer of 1998 this is what happened, that the villagers organised their own defence and had their own commander. This is what happened mainly in the villages where the horizontal organisation took place and there was no connection vertically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But where you said that where the KLA was better organised in a certain village or a certain area, that the commanders -- commander was not elected by the villagers. How was he appointed? How did he get his position as a commander? Was he appointed by higher level of KLA or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, Drenica was better organised and usually the appointment of commanders in these villages was done through a proposal by the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Through the proposal of the zone and then received the approval of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I then go on to ask you some specific questions about Dukagjin and put some propositions to you. If you don't know the answers, please say so. But first of all, Mr. Krasniqi, in the witness statement you've made in this case at paragraph 7, there is a sentence which reads: "The subzones, including Drenica and Dukagjin, existed on paper as early as 1995." Now, can I understand, please, what did you mean by that expression "existed on paper as early as 1995"?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant that they existed on paper, but in reality the situation on the ground was completely different. I also said it earlier that there was a period when we had two KLAs: One on paper, our wishful thinking, what we wanted the KLA to be; and the KLA that existed on the ground. So there was a big difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, we've heard evidence of witnesses in this case and indeed seen documents that record the emergence of organisation in the Dukagjin region. And I just want to put some propositions to you. I'm going to suggest to you, first of all, that within Dukagjin, the village defence organisation that you've described as characteristic were first brought together in a meeting on the 26th of May, 1998, when four small subzones, as they were called, were created in the villages along the Peje to Decan and Gjakove road; in other words, the villages to the east side of that road, grouping together into four relatively small subzones. Now, were you aware that, first of all, that there was a meeting at the end of May in which some attempt was made for the first time to coordinate village defences in the Dukagjin region?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember this occasion in May, but later on I remember that the villagers in the Dukagjin area had their meetings and appointed their commanders or elected their commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this is what I was going to come to. About a month later on the 23rd of June, I suggest the Dukagjini Plain Operational Zone was established at a meeting attended by Rexhep Selimi, and at which Ramush Haradinaj was elected as zone commander. Does that accord with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And can I suggest to you that even after that there were areas within the broad Dukagjini Plain that were not properly incorporated into any organised structure and that, for example, Bislim Zyrapi was dispatched in mid-July to seek to improve coordination in the Dukagjini region?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Bislim Zyrapi was at the time in the Dukagjin area.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And do you agree that it was known that there were problems of coordination in that area?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were problems at the time between the zone commander that had been appointed, Ramush Haradinaj, and the commander that was elected later on by the villager who was Tahir Zemaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think that's an incident or a series of incidents that occurred in July. Generally speaking, were there problems of communication, for example, with the area to the west of the main road close to the border?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look at those interview notes again for a moment, and could you turn to paragraphs 82 to 84 and just read them over to yourself, please. Yes? Can I ask you, please, first of all, is it correct, then, that the first time you met Mr. Haradinaj was at the end of June/beginning of July; that was the first occasion you'd met?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And was that the first occasion on which you became aware that he had any commanding role in the Dukagjini area?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I knew this from before, before I went.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Would it coincide with his appointment on the 23rd of June, approximately?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask you to look briefly at paragraph 81 in those notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What would coincide exactly with the appointment?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This witness's knowledge of Mr. Haradinaj having a commanding role was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just check, one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think it starts at line 19, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Sorry, while Presiding Judge is checking it, do we have a translation in the electronic system of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: An English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, of the interview?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, an electronic copy and I think also a hard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it has not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I did not get --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- been assigned a number since you are not going to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we usually consult those documents that are tendered and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. [Trial Chamber and registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since the question is there, if there's -- we don't have a hard copy, we could just try to consult that, but I don't know whether we have access to the lists of uploaded documents which are not yet --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I did hand in to Your Honours a hard copy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the English, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Judge Hoepfel is asking for the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the original is English, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The original is English.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the translation which the witness has in front of him which I do understand is a translation in his own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which he --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: He --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- has signed at some stage --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: He has at some stage signed the Albanian translation, and not the one -- there's no signature on the document he has but he has testified in the past he has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Judge Hoepfel is trying to have access to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I will ensure that a copy is available certainly after the next break, and if those following the transcript in the Defence room can pick this point up, it may well be in sooner than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And let's go back to --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Paragraph 81 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to where I ... Yes. Just to be sure, since when, Mr. Krasniqi, were you aware of or when had you become aware that Mr. Haradinaj had any commanding role in the Dukagjini area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must have been in July.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It must have been in June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember the exact date, but it must have been late June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to go -- I have to concentrate. One second, please. You said -- you confirmed when asked by Mr. Emmerson that it was at the end of June/beginning of July that you -- that was the first occasion you had met with Mr. Haradinaj. And then you were asked: "And was that the first occasion on which you became aware that he had any commanding role in the Dukagjini area?" And you said: "No. I knew this from before, before I went." How much time before you went you became aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult for me now to pinpoint the time, but when I set off to go to the Dukagjin area, to Jabllanice, I thought that I was going to meet Ramush Haradinaj, who was the zone commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that's not -- that's not a real answer to my question. When you went, it's clear that you -- or would you say that you -- while going there, you had become aware of his commanding role. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that he was a fighter and member of the KLA. I knew this from before, but after I became spokesperson of the KLA I went to the Dukagjin area and I knew at the time that the zone commander was Ramush Haradinaj, because he had been appointed by the General Staff. So I knew that he was the zone commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you said: "Well, that he was a fighter and a member of the KLA," you knew that from before. Was he like any other KLA fighter or any other KLA member or did, in your perception from these earlier days, did he have any -- was he of any prominence as a fighter or a KLA member or was he, from what you learned, only an ordinary KLA member or ordinary fighter? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On the 24th of March there was a battle in the village of Gllogjan between the members of the KLA and the Serbian police, and the name I heard after the event of the 24th of March. But I contacted him in June because after these things and events happened, he was appointed commander. Whether it was the 23rd or the 24th of June, I can't tell you, but I know that it was late June 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that, but when you said: "The name I heard after the event of the 24th of March," was that just a name of a fighter or a KLA member or did you hear this name in relation to a prominent member or a leading member? I mean, I'm just trying to find out whether before Mr. Haradinaj was appointed and you visited him, whether you learned, when you learned his name, whether that was related to any prominent position he may have had as a fighter or as a KLA member.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the beginning when the fighting occurred, especially in early June, as far as the Dukagjini Zone was concerned, our first man as member of the General Staff was Lahi Brahimaj. So I learned of Ramush Haradinaj as a name through Lahi Brahimaj. But my first contact with him was end of June/early July, as I've pointed out earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could you look at paragraph 81 of your interview notes there, please. First sentence in that paragraph, I'm going to read the English sentence into the record quotation. "When asked if the commander of an operational zone would know what was happening in his area of responsibility, Mr. Krasniqi stated that they did, in fact, try to know but this at times proved difficult." Was that a true statement that you made in that interview?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you turn to paragraph 75, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: At paragraph 75 in the English reads: "Mr. Krasniqi stated that around the 11th of June, 1998, the KLA was functioning mainly in units with limited communication between them, this being a security measure where the units would act as independent cells." First of all, was that a true statement also, Mr. Krasniqi, of the situation as you understood it to be when you took over as spokesman?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I wonder if you can clarify just one matter of potential confusion that arises in some of these communiques. We see, in some of the early communiques, references to operational zones 1 and 5, and that was a reference that can be found, for the record, in annex 5. During your testimony in Limaj, you identified those two zones I think as Llap and Drenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drenica was zone number 1, while number 5 was Llap.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: As of December 1997 when these zones existed essentially on paper; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think I've explained this earlier. Up until November 1998, Drenica, Llap, Dukagjin were qualified as subzones. Kosova was considered as one zone and there were other zones outside Kosova. By the end of 1998, the General Staff changed its policy and its main operational zone was Kosova with its seven operational zones. So from this point on the subzones are called zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could you just look at annex 5 for a moment, please, and you will find a passage that you need to look at. In the box on the right-hand side of the article in annex 5, the vertical box on the right-hand side in the second paragraph, and we have it in the second paragraph as well beginning: "On the evening ..." Now, there are references in those lines to operational zone 5 and operational zone 1. Those areas, I think, you gave evidence in Limaj were Llap and Drenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. During this period, maybe there was a confusion between subzones and zones, but during this period of time the entire territory of Kosova was considered as one zone. I'm speaking about the time when this communique was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So am I, Mr. Krasniqi. I don't want to take a great deal of time over this, but you gave evidence about this in the Limaj case, and it's transcript 3323, about this very communique and said that the reference there to operational zone number 5 was a reference to Llap and the reference to operational zone number 1 was a reference to Drenica. And I think if you look at the context, that must be right, mustn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Does it appear then that the author of this communique is a bit confused as between subzones --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Emmerson, to interrupt. I'm not clear, this last answer of the witness: "As I said earlier," I'm not sure what that answer refers to. If we could seek some clarification at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I understand what your evidence is about the organisation of zones, but with this passage here in this communique, when asked about it in Limaj, you agreed that it was a reference to Llap and Drenica. Now, just so that we're clear, in the context of that report of that communique, does it appear that it is a reference to Llap and Drenica?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that particular time, no, but if you look it from a later perspective, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. All I'm trying to ascertain is it appears that the author of this communique is referring to those areas as operational zones rather than subzones, does it not?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want to move on now to another topic, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you look at the clock, Mr. Emmerson --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I would suggest that we have a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. I -- I think I've probably got no more than another 15 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but nevertheless that would take us too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No. I'm just giving Your Honour an indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that concluding your cross-examination would take you 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: 15 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15 minutes or so. Could the other Defence counsel give me an indication on how much time they would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey will be going after Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I will be taking about 20 minutes, I think, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, you stand the last in the row.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think I will be taking the balance of the time, however much time that leaves me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would then -- that's clear. We will have a break, Mr. Krasniqi, and we'll resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, could you turn again to those interview notes and familiarise yourself with paragraphs 22 and 23, please, of your interview notes. And I want to ask you some questions now on the subject of collaborators. First of all, once you've found the relevant paragraphs, I'll just read into the record the English translation, and this is again you commenting on the article carrying an interview in Der Spiegel from the 6th of July. Paragraph 22 reads: "Mr. Krasniqi was asked to explain the references made to collaborators in this article to which he responded that he made the comments but that they were part of the referred 'Psychological warfare' aimed at preventing civilians from serving the Serbian regime." Paragraph 23: "Mr. Krasniqi agreed that this term collaborator and these type of references stating retaliation against them appeared as a repetitive theme in many of the KLA communiques issued. However, he said that they should be interpreted in the context in which they were published as part of the referred 'propaganda campaign'." Pausing there, please, and allowing the translation to catch up. Mr. Krasniqi, was that a truthful account that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor of the references that you made in your interviews?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When you gave evidence in the Limaj trial, Mr. Krasniqi, you described your understanding of the word or the concept of a collaborator as a person who was actively recruited to work for the Serb security services or a little later on, recruited within the ranks of the Serb forces, military, and police forces. Was that your understanding of the term "collaborator," Mr. Krasniqi, when you used it?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although this term is a foreign term originating from Norway or France used there after the Second World War. These were people who in the case of Kosova served the apparatus of the Milosevic regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But just to be clear, when you used the expression "collaborator," are you referring to somebody who has been recruited into the Serb security services or the police or the military?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could you turn, please, to annex number 7 in the blue file --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I'd like to make sure that I fully understand the last answer of the witness. If you say, "someone who has been recruited into the Serb security services or the police or the military," would that in your understanding exclude someone who was not recruited but who would render services to the Serb security services or the Serb police or the Serb military, so would assist them in performing their task without being recruited. Would you still call them or not call them collaborators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They would not be collaborators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Only those that were part of the repressive apparatus of the Serbian police and military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to give you an example. If someone, for example, would provide information, although not being recruited, to the Serb military forces about KLA positions, would you consider such a person to be a collaborator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These persons that were not recruited, there was no way that we could know that they were collaborators. We referred to those who were recruited, who were serving in this apparatus and those for whom we had information. Maybe there were others for whom we did not have information that they were in the service of this apparatus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I would tell you that this Chamber has received testimony in which it is said that there were suspicions about certain persons providing information to the Serbs, so therefore that such suspicions could even exist where there's no evidence or at least it is not said that these persons were recruited but just gave their assistance, would you still say that you could not know of such persons because they had not been recruited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I make it clear. My questioning was directed to this witness's use of that term and therefore to the understanding that we should attach to it when he uses it. May I just make that clarification clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. At the same time --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- one of the last answers the witness gave was about logic --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What one could know and what one could not know. And that's, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand entirely. I wasn't querying the question at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we look at tab 7, please, as an example of the use of the term "collaborator," although not, I think, by you. This is a communique -- a report, I'm sorry, in Pristina Bujku on the 28th of February, 1998. Now, Mr. Krasniqi, you will find the relevant passage that I need to ask you about just over halfway down page 1 in the Albanian, and it begins: "On the 23rd of January, 1998 ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And we have it roughly, Your Honours, opposite the hole-punch, I think, slightly above it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And there's a passage there that reads and I will quote it for the record: "On the 23rd of January, 1998, our units carried out an attack on the criminal Desimir Vasic, a close collaborator of Arkan." Now, pausing there for a moment. Arkan, I think is a name we're all familiar with, and was the leader of a Serbian paramilitary organisation called the Tigers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: These were irregular forces responsible for some of the worst violence in Croatia and in Bosnia, and in Kosovo; is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did they use and incorporate individuals, whether Serbian or any other ethnicity, inside Kosovo, did they absorb, for example, Kosovo Serbs into their ranks, paramilitary groups like that, as far as you understood the position?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably they were included in those forces, but I don't know any others except for this name here. Personally, I didn't know any person in concrete terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But do you know anything about Desimir Vasic? Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But in general terms if a Kosovo Serb was recruited into one of the paramilitary groups, you would describe that as an individual who had been recruited into the Serbian military forces and as a collaborator, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This one couldn't have been a collaborator. He was a member. He was a Serb. We referred with the term "collaborator" to the Albanians who served -- who rendered services to the repressive Serbian regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, then the word "collaborator" seems to have been used here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Emmerson, if you would allow me to make one observation about the word "collaborator." Looking at different languages in which it is used, to the extent I have knowledge of those languages, it could have - but please correct me when you have a different view - "collaborer" in French could be working together, which is the literal meaning of the word, and it has also a defamatory meaning, that is, working together with the enemy. I am not quite sure to what extent the translation -- the word used here, "collaborator," reflects the -- a more neutral original word or the defamatory original. I'm -- perhaps if --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I ask the witness in relation to the Albanian, whether the word used is the same as would be used for someone who had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And especially the same as he used in the other documents -- that was used in the other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you look, Mr. Krasniqi, at the Albanian sentence, can you find the word there that describes the relationship between Desimir Vasic and Arkan. How is that relationship described in the Albanian, please? Could you read that for us and we'll have it translated. Perhaps just read the line beginning: "On the 23rd of January ..." down to "Arkan," for us and the translators will pay particular attention to the word we're interested in. Would you read it out for us.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 23rd of January, 1998, our units launched an attack against criminal Desimir Vasic, a close collaborator of Arkan." Here it is not used in the sense of a collaborator, but more in the sense of an associate, a member of the Arkan's forces. So here it does not have the meaning of the word "collaborator." Usually we use this term when a person helps the enemy who is of another nationality or religion. As I said, this term originated from Norway and France and -- after the Second World War, and was later used in other parts of Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you turn, please, in this context to the interview notes again and to paragraph 69 so that we have a sense as to how you understood the term, Mr. Krasniqi. I'm going to read into the record the English translation of paragraph 69. Perhaps you will follow it in the Albanian. "Mr. Krasniqi stated that the General Staff stressed frequently that the KLA must obey and respect the international norms and not target civilians. He additionally stressed that to his knowledge no collaborators were arrested and executed. Some may have been killed, but that would have happened during battle at the front line, never after detention." Is that an accurate record of what you told the Prosecution, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And is it an accurate record of your understanding of the position?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, just for your information, the word used in the original, annex 7, and in this paragraph 69 seems to be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the extent I can decipher that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And two final topics, if I may. I want to ask you just about one aspect of your testimony in Limaj in relation to civilians, generally, as military targets. This is Limaj transcript 3387, line 24, concerning the position of Serb civilians. And you said this: "Because as KLA, as armed people, we could have organised attacks on Serb population and villages in many parts of Kosova, but all over the time, during all of the war this has never happened, even in a single instance." First of all, Mr. Krasniqi, was that evidence that you gave on oath in the Limaj case true?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Were there Serb civilian villages, pockets of -- concentration of Serb civilians in different parts of Kosovo during 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And were they attacked, the civilian enclaves, by the KLA forces?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single instance during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally this --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And for this I need to go into private session, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Then I further draw the attention that in paragraph 23 of the notes it seems that we find at least the same word. Whether it has different meanings or not is another matter, but it seems that the same expression is used in all three places where it is translated by "collaborators." Mr. Harvey -- yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Harvey does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I gave a number in private session in respect of a particular individual and I gave Your Honours the wrong number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think I can give the right number in open session because the context -- well, perhaps not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kearney, the commitment you made in respect of a witness with a certain number, where -- would that extend to the number Mr. Emmerson will now give us -- no, perhaps, let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would rather do it at the very end, Mr. Emmerson, that's better. I have to read two decisions anyhow. We'll then invite the witness to -- the witness to leave the courtroom already so that in both directions that we keep confidentiality ensured. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krasniqi, or good evening, perhaps. I am representing Lahi Brahimaj, whom of course you got to know as colleagues on the General Staff after you became spokesperson in June of 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And, in fact, before you became spokesperson in June of 1998, you didn't know Lahi Brahimaj at all, did you?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Indeed, until at least March of 1998, your public persona was that of -- you were a member of the Presidency of the LDK in Drenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: In fact, in the Limaj transcript it appears as a member of the Presidency of the LDK in Drenoc [sic], but in fact it should be Drenica, should it not?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drenas in Gllogoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Oh, Drenac [sic] in Gllogoc.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Drenas and the official name is Gllogoc, the official name used in the administration, the UNMIK administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. You officially broke with the LDK after the massacre -- massacres in Prekaze and Likoshan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You've already told the Tribunal today that until June of 1998, others in the KLA General Staff did not know you, and that was because, of course, of your public position. Rather than publicising your association with the KLA, you were publicly an LDK man; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And you would not be surprised to learn that Lahi Brahimaj had no idea that you had anything to do with the General Staff until your public announcement on the 11th of June of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know this, I did not know him, and if Lahi did not know me, he can say that for himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a little about the conditions under which you were operating with the General Staff in the middle of 1998 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And perhaps it would be helpful in this regard if we could have D37, a map of the Drenica area, on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: First of all, while we're waiting for that to come up, Mr. Krasniqi, is it correct that the General Staff at this period did not have any one specific building out of which it was operating? I'm talking about when -- after you had joined in June of 1998.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until June 1998, the staff did not have one specific building where they met. But after I was appointed spokesperson, the meetings of the General Staff were held generally at the place where I was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And that was, remind us, please?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 10th of June onwards, after I was appointed spokesperson, the meetings of the General Staff were held mainly, not always but mainly, where I was based, because I was the public person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: My question is: Where were you based?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the public announcement, two or three meetings were held in my own home, in my neighbourhood, also in houses of my relatives. Then after my appointment, the meetings were held in Klecke, Divjake, Fshati i Ri or Novo Selle, and Negrovce. All these villages are in the Berisha mountains, while Lladroc is in the southern part of these mountains. They are in the map as well, you can see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I think we can see Klecke almost immediately due south of the red triangle of Berisha, and then to the west of Klecke we see Lladroc. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: To the north-east of Klecke we see Divjake?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And if we continue -- sorry. If we continue on almost in a line from Klecke through Divjake we get to Negroc?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negrovce is in the north-western part of the Berisha mountains --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: North-eastern part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And so -- sorry, Novo Selle is not marked on this map. Is that close to -- can you give us an indication of a town that it's close to or a village that it's close to?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a red dot here and the triangle which says Berisha, close to Berisha, to the south, is the village of Novo Selle or Fshati i Ri. It is close to the Berisha village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to make matters clear, so that is Novo Selle entirely different from the Novo Selle north of Pec.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's a different one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because one appears on the map -- of the maps that have ever been shown to us and the other does not. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a little about where you stayed. Did you always stay in your own home during this period after June when you became the public spokesperson, or did you have to live essentially underground?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I became spokesperson, I went to my village from time to time because along this line to the north, after Berisha you have Arlat and after Arlat you have Negrovce. There is a rectangle there coloured in red. However, most of the time I spent in Divjake, Klecke, in Javor which is to the south-east of Klecke, and Javoc [phoen]. I also went to other villages in Drenica, but mainly I stayed in the villages I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that other members of the General Staff like you were also moving around constantly from one place to another for security reasons?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they moved for security reasons and they were not made public because of security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: After you joined - I'm going to take it from June 11th onwards - how frequently would you be in contact with Lahi Brahimaj? Would it be, should we say, on a weekly basis, a daily basis, or a monthly basis? How frequently? Should we say between -- for the first month of your membership of the General Staff -- your public membership of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the first month we met more often because there was not too much fighting going on in Kosova. We were in a phase of trying to consolidate the General Staff, and Lahi Brahimaj was staying for a longer time in this part of Drenica. So we saw each other more often. So when Lahi was staying in these villages in Drenica, we met more often, more frequently, while when he was in the Dukagjini area, we did not meet that frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: The General Staff divided responsibilities between the political and the operative areas of responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You, of course, were in the political. To whom did you report directly?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each department had a chief, and the head of the department -- of the political department was Hashim Thaqi. This department informed the General Staff on political issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Lahi Brahimaj would have been on the operative side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lahi Brahimaj was - how can I put it? - he was head of financial and economic issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And was he, therefore, reporting to Sokol Bashota and Rexhep Selimi?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because they had higher positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Now, you visited Jabllanice on two occasions. Would that be correct? One in around about the middle of July - I'm not going to put a precise date on it - and the second time about the 7th of September. First of all, do you agree that you were in Jabllanice on two occasions, roughly those dates?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And when you visited Jabllanice, did you see the barracks there where the soldiers stayed?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And on the occasions when you were there, would it be fair to say there were probably something in the region of 20 or more soldiers stationed in those barracks?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I went there, there were more soldiers, I think. In Jabllanice at the time there was also a field hospital where there were some wounded soldiers. But the first time, as I already mentioned, there were more soldiers in Jabllanice. They were better organised. The second time when I went there, after the summer offensive and after the defeat that the KLA suffered because of people who deserted, Tahir Zemaj's people who deserted and went to Albania, the KLA at the time in Jabllanice had only 30 soldiers, approximately, and Jabllanice was surrounded by police and military Serb forces. The situation was very difficult at the time in the Dukagjin area for the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I certainly accept everything you said about that. That would have been around the 7th of September, that visit; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Going back to the earlier visit in July, you say there were more soldiers on that occasion than the 30 or so whom you saw in September. Approximately how many soldiers did you see, do you think, in July? Again, I'm not asking for a precise figure.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an exact figure, but there were many soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Now, when you gave an answer earlier today to the Tribunal that "When it came to contact in the Dukagjin Zone, Lahi Brahimaj was the person I knew and the person I communicated with. I think he was responsible for the area at the time." Do you recall giving that answer to the Prosecutor earlier on today?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was not only responsible for the area at the time, but he was also a member of the General Staff of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, I want to explore what you mean by "responsible for the area." He was, of course, a staff officer on the General Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And as a staff officer on the General Staff, would you agree he was not in a position to be a command officer on the ground in the Dukagjin Zone at the same time?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When you say that he was somebody who was responsible for the area, is that in the sense that within the General Staff when you would have a meeting of the General Staff to receive reports from different zones, he would be somebody who would be consulted because he had a specialised knowledge of the Dukagjin area?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Because, of course, you knew, as Mr. Emmerson has already questioned you about, that Ramush Haradinaj from the 23rd of June at least onwards was the commander of the zone?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And so, when you said again earlier, I'm going to quote you, if I may: "In the beginning when the fighting occurred, especially in early June, as far as the Dukagjini Zone is concerned our first man as member of the General Staff was Lahi Brahimaj. So I learned of Ramush Haradinaj as a name through Lahi Brahimaj." When you gave that answer earlier today, was that again in this same context, that when fighting started, you in your position as spokesperson for the KLA on the political side, you automatically went to Lahi Brahimaj because he was there with you in Drenica and said, basically, "Lahi, brief me on what's going on in the Dukagjin Zone."

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, because he was a member of the General Staff and it was logical that I would address him first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, I just turned myself off. Thank you. Communications were not only by telephone, you said in answer to a question from Mr. Kearney earlier today. Was that because it was dangerous -- it was considered dangerous to use the telephones too much because they were tapped by the Serb intelligence agencies?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course they were tapped. And in order to escape from this tapping, we tried to use the satellite telephones. Sometimes the reception was not good. Whenever we could, we sometimes went physically to meet a person that we needed to meet or sometimes we also used a courier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm going to turn now briefly to my last topic with you, and that concerns --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey, before you do so --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll not finish with the witness today anyhow. How much time would you still need? I have to read two decisions and we have to go into private session for the matter we discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm happy to pause here and resume in the morning. I may need ten minutes, it may be less than that. I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then for tomorrow then you would need ten minutes. I have tried to calculate, Mr. Guy-Smith, when you said, "I'd use the time remaining," that would be approximately 40, 45 minutes, that was my calculation at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was my calculation, too. I believe I need about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would give us half an hour. Mr. Kearney, I did understand that you would need ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: No more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That brings us tomorrow to finish well within the time of the first session. Then, Mr. Krasniqi, we'll have to deal with a few procedural matters, but we're not going to bother you with that, Mr. Krasniqi. I'd like to give you the same instructions as I did yesterday, that is, that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony already given or still to be given. And we'd like to see you back tomorrow, quarter past 2.00 in afternoon, and if I'm not mistaken, Madam Registrar, this same courtroom. Yes. Madam Usher, could you escort Mr. Krasniqi out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd first like to turn into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then. In relation to the present witness, Mr. Krasniqi, the transcripts in the Limaj case of the testimony of this witness are admitted into evidence. As far as the nine attached documents are concerned, Mr. Kearney, the Chamber would prefer that you would provide for admission clear copies -- I mean clean copies. Because now the nine documents attached to the transcript bear P numbers, but P numbers of the Limaj case, which could easily create all kinds of confusion. So therefore, we'd like to separate the transcript in the Limaj case and then have not nine documents but eight documents because attachment 5 is the same as already attached to the statement of this witness. So the Chamber would then expect you to provide us with eight clean copies not bearing the numbers in the Limaj case in order to avoid confusion. Then I've got two decisions I'd like to deliver. The first one is a decision, the Trial Chamber's decision, on protective measures for Witness 6. On the 25th of May, 2007, the Prosecution applied for the trial-related protective measures of pseudonym, and face and voice distortion for Witness 6. The witness and his family live in Kosovo. The witness has expressed fear for his safety and that of his family should it become publicly known that he gave evidence for the Prosecution. On the 29th of May, 2007, the Chamber put on the record that the Defence did not oppose the motion. The party seeking protective measures for a witness, which in this case is the Prosecution, must demonstrate an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or the witness's family should it become known that the witness has given evidence before the Tribunal. This standard can be satisfied by showing that a threat was made against the witness or the witness's family, or by demonstrating a combination of the following three factors: One, the witness's testimony may antagonise persons who reside in a specific territory; two, the witness or his or her family live or work in the territory, have property in that territory, or have concrete plans to return to live in the territory; and three, there exists an unstable security situation in that territory, which is particularly unfavourable to witnesses who appear before the Tribunal. According to the Prosecution, Witness 6 received threats in the past. He was granted protective measures at the pre-trial stage. The Prosecution has not reported on any new threats directed against Witness 6. Nevertheless, given the nature of the witness's testimony, the Chamber is satisfied that it may antagonise persons who reside in Kosovo. The Chamber also notes that the witness and his family live in Kosovo and do not wish to be relocated for reasons that are understandable for the Chamber. The Chamber takes this opportunity to inform the parties that it accepts their agreement that there exists an unstable security situation in Kosovo, which is particularly unfavourable to witnesses who appear before the Tribunal. This agreement can be found on the transcript pages 3955 and 3956. As the three conditions of the test are met, the Trial Chamber grants the Prosecution's request for pseudonym and face and voice distortion. And this concludes the Trial Chamber's decision on protective measures for Witness 6. I'd like to deliver one other decision, and it has some urgency, that's why it might take us three minutes or four minutes past 7.00, that is a decision on the Prosecution's motion of the 7th of May, 2007, for the admission pursuant to Rule 92 ter of Witness 12's transcript and related exhibits in the Limaj case. That transcript consists of 137 pages, and there is a total of two exhibits, both of which are maps. The Prosecution in paragraphs 2 and 3 of its motion identifies certain topics which are, according to the Prosecution "extremely probative and highly relevant" to this case. The footnotes refer to half a dozen pages of transcript. However, the Prosecution apparently does not limit its submission to these pages and asks for the whole transcript to be admitted. Having read the whole of the witness's transcript in the Limaj case, the Chamber considers that the Prosecution has not sufficiently demonstrated that the bulk of the evidence contained therein is relevant and has probative value, since it mostly covers incidents which are outside the scope of the indictment in the present case, such as several meetings with Commander Celiku, also known as Fatmir Limaj. In particular, the Chamber has found about 30 pages with direct relevance to the present case and less than 20 pages relating to the background of the armed conflict, which leaves more than 80 pages whose relevance to the present case is unclear or doubtful. The Chamber invites the Prosecution to specify the exact pages of the transcript which it considers relevant to the present case and why they are relevant. The Prosecution is given 24 hours to do so. The Chamber wishes to add a few policy remarks which the parties may find useful as guidance. Even though Rule 92 ter does not exclude admission of written evidence that goes to the acts or conduct of the accused, the present Chamber prefers that the Prosecution elicits evidence that is central and critical to the present case viva voce. This ensures that the Chamber is better able to understand evidence of this kind it admits. Thus, if the Limaj transcript contains such evidence, the witness should be additionally examined on it viva voce. The Prosecution should, in general, take great care not to flood the Chamber with information whose utility is not apparent to the Chamber or which is of insufficient relevance to this case. This concludes the Chamber's decision. Although it's not usual to comment on decisions, I hope that it's well understood that the viva voce examination of a witness on these kind of topics is in addition to admission of 92 ter statements dealing with the same matter. It's just the Chamber does not want solely on basis of the written statement or the written transcripts gain an impression and gain an understanding of the testimony the witness -- the evidence the witness gives. We adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom.
